planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring directly into permanently saturated soil; this boreal native resents drying out even briefly and establishes fastest in cool conditions.

directions: Site this rhizomatous native in a bog garden, streambank, or pond margin with consistently saturated, cool soil and dappled shade; it is far more cold-hardy than the showier Asian Petasites species, tolerating the short, harsh growing seasons of its boreal range from Alaska across Canada to the northern Great Lakes. Flower stalks topped with creamy-white clusters emerge directly from the rhizome in earliest spring before the large, arrow-shaped leaves unfurl, distinguishing it from the rounder-leaved P. frigidus. Give it room to roam since the rhizomes travel steadily in wet ground, and use it as a coarse-textured foliage foil for sedges and ferns rather than in a small, contained bed. It spreads too readily for formal borders but excels in naturalized wet-shade plantings where its running habit is an asset.

common_name: Vedrariensis Lobelia (Veitch's Hybrid Blue Cardinal Flower)

planting.note: Divide and replant clumps in spring into reliably moist, humus-rich soil; shallow rooting means plants heave in winter if soil drains too freely.

directions: This long-cultivated hybrid between Lobelia cardinalis and L. siphilitica was raised at the Veitch nursery's Coombe Wood grounds in England in the early 1900s, its cultivar name a Latinized nod to that origin. Bronze-flushed foliage sends up tall, slender spikes of violet-blue flowers in late summer, bridging the color gap between its scarlet and true-blue parents. Grow it at a pond edge or in a rain garden where the crown never dries out; unlike many perennial borders, this one punishes neglectful watering with rapid foliage collapse. Lift and divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor and flower count.
